newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore OUB Bank 1996 net profit jumps 19.7 pct.
newsitem.headline: Singapore OUB Bank 1996 net profit jumps 19.7 pct.

text.p: Singapore's Overseas Union Bank Ltd oumb.si (OUB) said on Friday its net profit jumped 19.7 percent to Singapore $310.4 million (US$217 million) in 1996, up from S$259.3 million in 1995.

Boosted by strong growth in its regional operations, particularly in Malaysia, and buoyant loans growth at home, the bank's total interest income rose to S$1.94 billion last year, compared with S$1.53 billion the year before.
Net interest income jumped 23.2 percent to S$678.2 million, OUB's President and Chief Executive Officer Peter Seah told a news conference.
"We are very pleased with the results," Seah told reporters, adding that they were in line with analysts' expectations.
He said analysts' predictions of "high teens" net profit growth to around S$360 million for 1997 were "possible".
"I'm quite optimistic for the prospects for the bank," Seah said. "We have been able to perform according to expectations over the last couple of years and hope that we can do that again," he added.

The bank proposed a rights issue of 137.66 million new shares on the basis on one new share for every five existing shares held. It said the issue was designed to increase its capital base to support expansion.
The group had shareholders funds of S$3.2 billion at the end of 1996, the bank said in a statement.
"Successful completion of the rights issue will raise shareholders funds to almost S$4 billion." it said.
"We feel that we need to further boost our capital for future expansion over the next few years," Seah said.
"This strong capital base is very important to us if we want to continue to operate actively in the region as a major provider of syndication."
OUB's loans and advances grew 28.5 percent in 1996, despite a slowdown in demand for financing housing purchases due to government measures to curb speculation in the Singapore property market.
Seah said he expected a further slowdown in loans to the housing market as a result of last year's measures and said this might mean slower overall growth in loans and advances.

"I would expect probably a smaller percentage of loan growth in 1997 in Singapore," he said. "I don't know if the strong loan growth which I expect from Malaysia will be able to compensate for slower Singapore loans growth."
"But slower loanns growth doesn't necessarily mean slower profit growth," he added.
The bank proposed a final dividend of 7.00 cents, unchanged from the year before. ($1 = S$1.43)
